query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-coating tungsten particles with a nanoscale nickel layer prior to composite consolidation will enhance copper wettability and interfacial bonding, thereby reducing void formation and phase separation in W–Cu composites and preserving mechanical durability under irradiation.
generation.material_initial_state: A pre-fabricated composite feedstock consisting of tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten regions dispersed within a copper matrix, as typically produced via vapor-coating of W powders.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin (20–50 nm) nickel coating to tungsten particles (using electroless plating, electroplating, or chemical vapor deposition) before mixing with copper, then consolidate the composite via spark plasma sintering at temperatures sufficiently below the Cu boiling point (e.g., below ~1200°C).
generation.conditions: Processing should be performed under a controlled, reduced atmosphere with a controlled heating profile to avoid Cu evaporation; the finalized composite is to be tested under cyclic thermal loads and simulated fusion irradiation conditions (e.g., neutron flux) at service temperatures well below Cu boiling point (2562 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: The nickel interlayer forms a chemically compatible, low-energy interface at the W–Cu boundary, promoting capillary infiltration and diffusive bonding that minimizes the formation of voids and defects.
generation.mechanism: Nickel acts as an interfacial promoter by reducing the surface energy mismatch between tungsten and copper. This improves the capillary action and diffusion at the interface during sintering, leading to a uniform microstructure with reduced porosity. It also serves as a diffusion barrier, mitigating intermetallic reactions that might further degrade thermal transport and mechanical stability under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to composites produced with vapor-coated W powders without the interfacial Ni layer, the Ni-coated composite is predicted to exhibit a lower void fraction, enhanced microstructural uniformity, improved thermal conductivity, and better mechanical integrity under cyclic thermal and irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: The baseline is W–Cu composites fabricated from vapor-coated W powders consolidated via spark plasma sintering without any interfacial modification.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable for fusion-reactor joint heat transfer components where processing temperatures are maintained below the boiling point of copper and service conditions involve high thermal flux and irradiation. Its effectiveness must be verified for composites consolidated below ~1200°C and tested under simulated fusion reactor irradiation and thermal cycling.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in void reduction, thermal conductivity, and mechanical durability remains uncertain until detailed microstructural and performance evaluations are performed; interfacial diffusion behavior under actual irradiation conditions may also introduce variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples under identical spark plasma sintering conditions: one set using tungsten particles pre-coated with a 20–50 nm Ni layer and a control set using uncoated tungsten particles. Conduct microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM, X-ray tomography) to quantify void fraction and interface quality, measure thermal conductivity using laser flash analysis, and perform mechanical tests (e.g., flexural or tensile strength) before and after exposing samples to simulated fusion irradiation and thermal cycling.
measurements: Void fraction and interfacial uniformity via SEM and X-ray tomography
Thermal conductivity using laser flash analysis
Mechanical durability through tensile or flexural testing
Performance before and after simulated irradiation/thermal cycling (dose and temperature monitoring)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated W–Cu composites do not show statistically significant improvements in reduced porosity, enhanced thermal conductivity, or superior mechanical properties relative to the uncoated control, the hypothesis will be rejected.
